ranking_outcomes.everyday_problem: Before anyone can solve a game, the model has to know what counts as better or worse for each person. The everyday version is simple: if a student chooses between two schedules, or a bidder chooses between money and an object, the model needs a consistent ranking of those outcomes before strategy can enter.
ranking_outcomes.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is representability. Preferences are qualitative rankings, but game theory often needs a number that preserves those rankings so the course can compare actions, lotteries, and expected payoffs.
ranking_outcomes.mathematical_lever: The lever is a utility representation and, under uncertainty, an expected-utility average. The number is useful because it lets later concepts ask whether one action gives a higher payoff than another under the same strategic conditions.
ranking_outcomes.why_it_matters: This subtheme prevents a common mistake: treating payoffs as arbitrary table decorations. They are the compressed statement of what each player is trying to achieve, and every equilibrium or auction result depends on them.
ranking_outcomes.first_principles_walkthrough: Start with ordinary preference: which outcome would the person choose if both were available? Then ask whether the ranking is consistent enough to be represented by a utility number. If chance enters, average the utility of each possible outcome by its probability rather than pretending uncertainty has disappeared.
ranking_outcomes.cross_links_and_limits: The same payoff ranking reappears in best response, bargaining, auctions, and Bayesian games. The limit is that ordinal preference and expected utility do different jobs; risk comparisons require more structure than a simple ranked list.
ranking_outcomes.lecture_evidence_chain: The preference, utility, and expected-utility evidence records anchor this subtheme in the opening lecture sequence, where the course builds the choice machinery used later.
ranking_outcomes.recognize_in_new_work: When a paper introduces values, rewards, costs, outside options, or welfare, ask what preference ranking those numbers represent and whether the later argument needs ordinal or cardinal structure.
ranking_outcomes.recognition_pattern: This subtheme is present whenever the paper spends early effort defining payoffs, welfare, costs, surplus, losses, or outside options before it starts solving the game. The tell is that the central dispute is not yet about clever strategy; it is about what each participant is trying to make larger, smaller, safer, or more likely.
ranking_outcomes.paper_reading_move: Translate every payoff number back into a sentence a person in the model could understand: I prefer this object to the money, I dislike this delay, I value safety more than upside, or I care about the other player's action. Then check whether the theorem uses only ranking information or also uses the size of payoff differences.
ranking_outcomes.boundary_test: The transfer breaks when the paper treats a convenient score as if it were a real preference. A model of bidding, bargaining, or policy choice can look precise while hiding risk attitudes, fairness concerns, external harms, budget limits, or a welfare weight that the people in the situation would not actually share.

tables_and_trees.everyday_problem: A social situation can be confusing because everyone’s outcome is created by several people at once. The course therefore needs pictures that keep the players, actions, timing, and payoffs visible.
tables_and_trees.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is representation discipline. A payoff table is good when timing can be ignored; a tree is needed when the order of moves or information at a decision point changes what a player can condition on.
tables_and_trees.mathematical_lever: The lever is the mapping from action profiles or histories to payoffs. Strategic form compresses simultaneous choices into profiles; extensive form expands the situation into nodes, branches, histories, and information sets.
tables_and_trees.why_it_matters: The representation often decides which solution concept is even meaningful. Dominance in a matrix, backward induction in a tree, and PBE in an information structure are not interchangeable visual styles.
tables_and_trees.first_principles_walkthrough: Ask whether players choose once without seeing each other, or whether someone observes, waits, or moves later. If timing has no strategic content, use the table. If later choices depend on earlier histories, draw the tree and preserve what each player knows at each node.
tables_and_trees.cross_links_and_limits: Tables connect to dominance and Nash equilibrium. Trees connect to backward induction, subgame perfection, bargaining, and PBE. The analogy breaks when a table hides a threat or a tree pretends players know histories they cannot observe.
tables_and_trees.lecture_evidence_chain: The strategic-form and extensive-form records support this subtheme directly. Later time-and-information records show why the early representational choice keeps mattering.
tables_and_trees.recognize_in_new_work: When reading a new model, inspect the representation first. Before trusting the theorem, ask what timing, observation, or payoff dependence the chosen representation has silently included or excluded.
tables_and_trees.recognition_pattern: This subtheme appears when the argument turns on the shape of the model: a normal-form table, an extensive-form tree, an information set, a history, a state, or a mapping from actions to outcomes. The clue is that changing the drawing would change what a player is allowed to know or condition on.
tables_and_trees.paper_reading_move: Before following any equilibrium calculation, redraw the situation in ordinary language. Who moves, what do they see, what can they remember, and which later choices depend on earlier choices? If the paper uses a table, ask why timing is harmless. If it uses a tree, ask which histories are actually distinguishable to the player. A useful check is to narrate one complete play of the game from start to finish; any fact you need during the narration must appear somewhere in the representation.
tables_and_trees.boundary_test: The analogy fails when the representation hides the strategic fact that matters most. A table can erase an incredible threat by making all choices look simultaneous. A tree can smuggle in information by separating nodes that the player could not tell apart. The model is only as honest as its information structure. Be especially suspicious when a paper says a representation is equivalent without explaining what observations, memories, and contingent choices are preserved.

eliminating_bad_moves.everyday_problem: Some games are cluttered with actions that no careful player would use. The everyday problem is how to remove obviously bad possibilities without already knowing exactly what everyone else will do.
eliminating_bad_moves.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is belief-free versus belief-based pruning. Dominance removes a move because another move beats it across opponent actions; rationalizability keeps a move if some defensible belief could make it optimal.
eliminating_bad_moves.mathematical_lever: The lever is comparison across opponent actions. Strict dominance checks an inequality in every relevant column or contingency, while iterated deletion repeats that comparison after earlier deletions shrink the game.
eliminating_bad_moves.why_it_matters: This subtheme teaches a lighter form of reasoning before full equilibrium. It shows that some behavior can be ruled out by internal inconsistency, but it also warns that deletion rules can depend on how strong the dominance notion is.
eliminating_bad_moves.first_principles_walkthrough: List one player’s possible actions. Compare two of them while holding each possible opponent action fixed. If one action is never worse and sometimes better, the inferior action has no strategic defense. After removing it, repeat the question because the strategic environment has changed.
eliminating_bad_moves.cross_links_and_limits: Pruning connects backward to payoff tables and forward to Nash equilibrium. It also connects to common knowledge because repeated deletion assumes players understand rationality and understand that others understand it. Weak dominance is the limit case where deletion order and interpretation can matter.
eliminating_bad_moves.lecture_evidence_chain: Dominance and iterated-deletion records anchor the mechanical pruning. Rationalizability records show where the course shifts from deleting bad moves to asking what beliefs can support surviving moves.
eliminating_bad_moves.recognize_in_new_work: Look for arguments that say a strategy is never used, cannot survive rationality, or is eliminated before equilibrium analysis. Then check whether the deletion is strict, weak, iterative, or belief-based.
eliminating_bad_moves.recognition_pattern: You are in this subtheme when the paper tries to simplify a game before solving it. The language may be about dominated strategies, admissibility, rationalizability, never-best responses, or actions no rational agent would choose. The common shape is a pruning argument: some branch of behavior is being declared strategically indefensible.
eliminating_bad_moves.paper_reading_move: Do the comparison yourself with the opponent's action held fixed. For each possible contingency, ask whether the allegedly bad move is worse than another available move. Then ask whether the deletion was made once, repeated after other deletions, or justified by a belief about what the opponent might do. Mark the exact assumption that licenses the deletion: strict inequality everywhere, common knowledge of rationality, or a belief that makes a surviving action optimal.
eliminating_bad_moves.boundary_test: This transfer is fragile around weak dominance and missing actions. If a strategy is only weakly worse, deleting it may erase equilibria or depend on deletion order. If the paper has already restricted the action set, a dominance argument may prove only that a move is bad inside an artificially small world. The safest audit is to ask what conclusion would survive if the deleted move remained available as a warning light.

stable_predictions.everyday_problem: A strategic prediction is fragile if one person can look at it and say, given what everyone else is doing, I should switch. The everyday problem is finding a forecast that survives that private check.
stable_predictions.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is mutual consistency. Each player’s action must be understandable as a best response to the others, so the prediction is held together by everyone’s incentives at once.
stable_predictions.mathematical_lever: The lever is the best-response condition. Nash equilibrium applies it to all players simultaneously; mixed strategies add probability weights when no fixed pure action can be stable.
stable_predictions.why_it_matters: This subtheme is the central bridge from story to prediction. It lets the course reject outcomes that sound plausible but contain a profitable one-person deviation.
stable_predictions.first_principles_walkthrough: First freeze what everyone else is doing. Ask what one player would choose. Do the same for each player. If the proposed profile passes every one of those checks, it is stable in the Nash sense; if not, the story has not earned prediction status.
stable_predictions.cross_links_and_limits: Stable prediction connects to dominance because dominated moves cannot be best responses. It connects to subgame perfection and Bayesian Nash when timing or hidden information changes what best response means. Stability still does not imply efficiency or fairness.
stable_predictions.lecture_evidence_chain: Best-response, Nash, and mixed-strategy records support the progression from one-player response to mutual consistency and then to randomization as a stability device.
stable_predictions.recognize_in_new_work: When a model claims an outcome, ask what deviation each participant has. If the paper never checks that question, it may be describing a desired outcome rather than an equilibrium.
stable_predictions.recognition_pattern: This subtheme shows up whenever a paper claims that a pattern of behavior is stable, self-enforcing, an equilibrium, or a fixed point of best responses. The plain sign is a no-regret check: each participant looks at everyone else's behavior and finds no single switch that would make them better off.
stable_predictions.paper_reading_move: Freeze the proposed behavior of everyone except one player. List that player's available deviations and compare payoffs. Repeat for every player and, in mixed settings, for every action that receives positive probability. A claimed equilibrium is not a mood of balance; it is a set of passed deviation tests. When probabilities appear, ask why the player is willing to randomize; the actions used with positive probability should leave that player equally well off.
stable_predictions.boundary_test: The idea breaks if the paper quietly changes the deviation set or ignores timing, information, or coalitions. Nash stability blocks one-person deviations at the modeled moment. It does not by itself prove social efficiency, fairness, robustness to mistakes, resistance to group deviations, or credibility after later histories. A good paper will say which notion of stability it needs and which stronger notions it is not claiming. If that caveat is absent, treat the prediction as local.

conflict_and_security.everyday_problem: In pure conflict, doing well means preparing for an opponent who benefits from your loss. The everyday problem is choosing a plan when the other side is actively trying to exploit it.
conflict_and_security.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is security under hostile response. A player should evaluate a move by the worst consequence an opponent can force, not by a friendly or average response.
conflict_and_security.mathematical_lever: The lever is maximin/minimax comparison. One side chooses the action or mixture with the best worst-case payoff, while the other side chooses the response that makes that payoff as small as possible.
conflict_and_security.why_it_matters: This subtheme clarifies a special but powerful case of equilibrium. In zero-sum games, strategic stability, value, and protection against exploitation line up more cleanly than in general games.
conflict_and_security.first_principles_walkthrough: Imagine announcing a plan to an adversary. For each plan, mark the worst payoff the adversary can force on you. Then choose the plan whose worst case is least damaging. Mixed strategies enter when predictability itself becomes exploitable.
conflict_and_security.cross_links_and_limits: Conflict-and-security connects to mixed strategies and best response. The limit is that many economic games are not zero-sum: cooperation, side payments, future interaction, or market design can make the security logic incomplete.
conflict_and_security.lecture_evidence_chain: Zero-sum and minimax records support this subtheme. Mixed-strategy evidence supplies the reason randomization can be protective in adversarial settings.
conflict_and_security.recognize_in_new_work: Look for language about value of a game, adversarial choice, robust guarantees, saddle points, or worst-case protection. Then check whether the setting is truly zero-sum or only being approximated that way.
conflict_and_security.recognition_pattern: This subtheme is active when the model treats the other side as someone who gains from your loss: matching pennies, inspection, security allocation, adversarial testing, or any setting with a value, saddle point, maximin, minimax, or exploitability claim. The ordinary sign is planning under a hostile reader of your plan.
conflict_and_security.paper_reading_move: For each proposed action, ask what the opponent would do after seeing enough to exploit it. Then compare the resulting worst cases, not the average cases you hope for. If randomization appears, read it as protection against being predictable rather than as psychological uncertainty. In a matrix, circle each row's worst entry and each column's best attack; the security argument is usually hiding in that simple inspection.
conflict_and_security.boundary_test: The transfer fails when conflict is only partial. Many institutional settings contain common gains, repeated relationships, side payments, reputation, or legal constraints. Treating them as zero-sum can make robustness look like the only virtue and hide designs that enlarge the joint surplus. Before accepting a minimax conclusion, ask who literally loses when the modeled player gains and whether any outside option can change that accounting. If both sides can improve together, the security frame is only one slice of the model, and the paper should justify why that slice dominates.

credible_time_paths.everyday_problem: Plans over time can fail because the person who promised a later action may not want to carry it out later. The everyday problem is separating real threats and promises from empty announcements.
credible_time_paths.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is sequential rationality. A plan must make sense not only at the start, but after every history where a player has to act.
credible_time_paths.mathematical_lever: The lever is backward recursion through a game tree. Terminal outcomes give values to final nodes; those values are pulled backward so earlier choices reflect credible later behavior.
credible_time_paths.why_it_matters: This subtheme explains why timing changes game theory. A Nash equilibrium can rest on a threat that would never be used, while subgame perfection and one-shot deviation tests remove those unstable time paths.
credible_time_paths.first_principles_walkthrough: Draw the last real decision first. Ask what the player would do there. Replace that part of the tree with its value, then move one step earlier. Continue until the start of the game inherits only choices that later players would actually want to carry out.
credible_time_paths.cross_links_and_limits: Credible time paths connect to bargaining because delay changes outside options and surplus division. They connect to repeated games because punishment must remain credible. They break when beliefs, hidden information, or renegotiation change the continuation values.
credible_time_paths.lecture_evidence_chain: Backward-induction, subgame-perfection, one-shot-deviation, and bargaining records support the core logic. Extensive-form evidence supplies the tree representation that makes the logic possible.
credible_time_paths.recognize_in_new_work: When a model contains threats, contracts, offers, punishments, or staged moves, inspect the continuation incentives. A prediction that only works at the initial node is not enough.
credible_time_paths.recognition_pattern: You are in this subtheme when the game unfolds through time and the paper relies on a future threat, promise, offer, refusal, punishment, or continuation plan. The central clue is that a statement made now has to be checked again later, after the history that activates it has actually happened.
credible_time_paths.paper_reading_move: Start at the last decision node and solve backward in everyday sentences: if we really got here, what would this player want to do now? Replace the later subgame with that answer and move one step earlier. Continue until every planned action is credible at the moment it would be chosen. Do not let an early promise do the work; make the continuation payoff at the later node carry the argument.
credible_time_paths.boundary_test: Backward reasoning is clean only when histories, payoffs, and information are clear. It weakens when players can renegotiate, care about reputation outside the tree, have hidden information, make mistakes, or face off-path beliefs that the model has not disciplined. A threat can be mathematically listed and still be behaviorally empty. The practical test is whether the threatened player, after the deviation has happened, still wants to pay the cost of punishment. If not, the path is a story, not a credible plan.

future_as_discipline.everyday_problem: People may want to cooperate, but a one-time temptation can be stronger than goodwill. The everyday problem is when tomorrow’s consequences can make today’s cooperation rational.
future_as_discipline.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is intertemporal incentive compatibility. Cooperation survives only if the discounted value of keeping the relationship outweighs the current gain from cheating.
future_as_discipline.mathematical_lever: The lever is a comparison between deviation gain and discounted punishment loss. Finite horizons often unravel because the final round has no future discipline; infinite or uncertain horizons can support trigger strategies.
future_as_discipline.why_it_matters: This subtheme explains how repeated play changes the set of possible outcomes. It is the course’s bridge from prisoner-dilemma-style failure to sustained cooperation, collusion, and folk-theorem multiplicity.
future_as_discipline.first_principles_walkthrough: Find the one-period gain from cheating. Then compute what the player loses if future partners punish that cheating. If the future loss, after discounting, is larger than the immediate gain, cooperation can be self-enforcing.
future_as_discipline.cross_links_and_limits: The future-as-discipline connects to credibility, because punishments must be worth carrying out, and to mechanisms, because repeated markets can generate informal rules. It breaks with impatience, poor monitoring, known final periods, or weak punishment capacity.
future_as_discipline.lecture_evidence_chain: Finite repetition, infinite repetition, folk theorem, and implicit cartel records support the progression from unraveling to future-enforced cooperation.
future_as_discipline.recognize_in_new_work: Look for discount factors, trigger strategies, repeated relationships, reputational incentives, or punishment paths. Then ask whether the future is strong and observable enough to discipline the present.
future_as_discipline.recognition_pattern: This subtheme appears when today's action is controlled by tomorrow's relationship: repeated games, collusion, reputation, trust, trigger strategies, monitoring, or a discount factor. The everyday sign is that a player could gain now by cheating, but might lose a stream of later benefits if others respond.
future_as_discipline.paper_reading_move: Separate the one-period temptation from the future punishment. Estimate what the player gains by deviating today, what future payoff is lost after punishment begins, and how much the player discounts that future. The model's cooperation claim lives or dies on that comparison. When a folk-theorem style result appears, read it as a feasibility claim with many possible equilibria, not as a prediction of which one people will actually coordinate on.
future_as_discipline.boundary_test: The transfer breaks when the future is not visible, not valuable, or not enforceable. Known final periods unravel backward. Noisy monitoring can punish innocent players or miss guilty ones. Impatient players may prefer immediate gain. Weak punishments can make a repeated relationship look more disciplined than it really is. Always ask who observes the deviation, how quickly they observe it, and why they would carry out the punishment afterward. Also ask whether the same future supports too many equilibria to make a sharp prediction without an added selection argument. Patience is discipline only when monitoring and response are credible.

hidden_types.everyday_problem: One side often knows something the other side cares about. A bidder knows her value, a worker knows ability, a sender knows type, or a player knows a private signal. The problem is how to reason before those facts are publicly known.
hidden_types.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is conditioning behavior on possible worlds. The model must say what types might exist, what each player believes about them, and what each type would choose.
hidden_types.mathematical_lever: The lever is expected payoff over types, plus Bayes-consistent updating in dynamic settings. A strategy is no longer one action; it can be a plan that tells each type what to do.
hidden_types.why_it_matters: This subtheme is what prevents private-information games from collapsing into complete-information fiction. It lets the course analyze auctions, signaling, reputation, and dynamic belief revision.
hidden_types.first_principles_walkthrough: List the hidden facts. Assign probabilities to them. For each type, ask which action gives the best expected payoff given beliefs about others. If actions are observed later, update beliefs when possible and check whether future behavior remains rational.
hidden_types.cross_links_and_limits: Hidden types connect to auctions through private values, to signaling through type-dependent messages, and to PBE through updated beliefs. The limit is that off-path beliefs and assumed priors can carry heavy modeling weight.
hidden_types.lecture_evidence_chain: Bayesian-game, types-and-beliefs, Bayesian-Nash, and PBE records support this subtheme’s move from static private information to dynamic belief consistency.
hidden_types.recognize_in_new_work: Look for types, priors, posteriors, private values, signals, or strategies indexed by hidden states. Then ask whether beliefs are disciplined by information or simply chosen to support the conclusion.
hidden_types.recognition_pattern: This subtheme is present when the same visible player could secretly be one of several kinds: high value or low value, strong or weak, informed or uninformed, honest or strategic. The model will use types, priors, signals, posteriors, private values, or strategies that depend on hidden facts.
hidden_types.paper_reading_move: Name the hidden fact before reading the equations. Then list what each type knows, what everyone else believes before observing behavior, what action each type would choose, and how beliefs should change after an observed signal. Keep asking whether the belief update follows from information or is merely convenient. A clean reading habit is to rewrite each strategy as if it says, if I am this type, I do this; if I am that type, I do that.
hidden_types.boundary_test: The transfer is dangerous when priors or off-path beliefs do too much work. A Bayesian model can make almost any story look disciplined if the type space, prior, or impossible-to-observe histories are chosen to fit the desired result. Private information should explain behavior, not serve as a hiding place for assumptions. Check whether a small change in prior beliefs would overturn the headline result. If it would, the conclusion is belief-sensitive rather than universal.

rules_for_bidding.everyday_problem: A seller, platform, or institution has to allocate scarce objects when participants know their own values and can shade what they reveal. The everyday problem is designing rules that still work when people act strategically.
rules_for_bidding.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is rule-induced incentives. A bid is not just a number; it is a response to the payment rule, allocation rule, beliefs about rivals, and sometimes quality or position effects.
rules_for_bidding.mathematical_lever: The lever is incentive compatibility and expected payment. Auction models compare how rules map bids and values into allocation probabilities and payments, then ask whether truthful or shaded bidding is optimal.
rules_for_bidding.why_it_matters: This subtheme turns game theory into market engineering. It explains why small rule changes can alter bidding behavior, seller revenue, efficiency, and platform outcomes.
rules_for_bidding.first_principles_walkthrough: Write the object being allocated, each bidder’s private value, the allocation rule, and the payment rule. Then stand in one bidder’s shoes and ask what bid maximizes payoff given beliefs about others and the consequences of winning.
rules_for_bidding.cross_links_and_limits: Rules for bidding connect to hidden types because values are private, and to stable prediction because bidding strategies must be equilibrium behavior. Revenue equivalence breaks when its assumptions fail; ad auctions add platform-specific constraints beyond textbook single-object auctions.
rules_for_bidding.lecture_evidence_chain: Auction, revenue-equivalence, and ad-auction records support the progression from basic bidding rules to equivalence results and sponsored-search design.
rules_for_bidding.recognize_in_new_work: Look for allocation rules, payment rules, bidding functions, reserve prices, quality scores, click probabilities, or truthful-reporting claims. Then check the incentive constraint that makes the rule work.
rules_for_bidding.recognition_pattern: This subtheme shows up when the paper designs or compares rules for allocating scarce goods: first-price auctions, second-price auctions, sponsored search, reserves, scoring rules, platform ranking, or mechanism-design claims. The visible object is a rule, but the real subject is how strategic people respond to that rule.
rules_for_bidding.paper_reading_move: Split the rule into three parts: who gets the object, what the winner or participants pay, and what information each participant has when choosing a bid. Then take one bidder's perspective and ask whether raising, lowering, or truthfully reporting the bid changes expected payoff. For platform auctions, also separate the bidder's value for attention from the platform's ranking score, because those two numbers need not reward the same behavior.
rules_for_bidding.boundary_test: Auction logic transfers poorly when textbook assumptions disappear. Budgets, risk aversion, correlated values, asymmetric bidders, quality scores, repeated platform interactions, and uncertain click behavior can break revenue equivalence or truth-telling claims. A mechanism's beauty is not enough; its incentive constraints must survive the market details. If the rule uses a proxy such as predicted clicks, ask who can manipulate the proxy and who bears the cost of bad matching. A good auction model makes those institutional details explicit.

messages_and_shared_awareness.everyday_problem: People talk, signal, announce, and observe public facts, but not every message should be believed and not every public fact coordinates action. The everyday problem is knowing when information actually changes behavior.
messages_and_shared_awareness.hidden_principle: The hidden principle is belief movement under incentives. Communication matters when it changes what receivers believe, and credibility depends on whether senders of different types would want to send different messages.
messages_and_shared_awareness.mathematical_lever: The lever is a belief system plus incentive constraints. Signaling uses costly or type-dependent actions; cheap talk uses payoff alignment; common knowledge uses repeated knowledge operators rather than ordinary private awareness.
messages_and_shared_awareness.why_it_matters: This subtheme explains the strategic life of information. It covers why education can signal ability, why advice may or may not persuade, and why coordination can require everyone to know that everyone else knows.
messages_and_shared_awareness.first_principles_walkthrough: Ask what the sender knows, what the receiver sees, what each type would prefer the receiver to believe, and whether the message or action is costly enough to separate types. For public facts, ask whether the fact is merely observed or mutually and repeatedly known.
messages_and_shared_awareness.cross_links_and_limits: Messages connect to hidden types and mechanisms through incentive compatibility. Common knowledge connects back to equilibrium because players may need shared awareness to coordinate on a strategy. The analogy breaks if costless talk is treated like costly signaling.
messages_and_shared_awareness.lecture_evidence_chain: Signaling, cheap-talk, and common-knowledge records support this subtheme, with signaling carrying type revelation, cheap talk carrying incentive-aligned persuasion, and common knowledge carrying coordination through higher-order awareness.
messages_and_shared_awareness.recognize_in_new_work: Look for messages, signals, announcements, disclosure, persuasion, public information, or higher-order belief claims. Then ask what incentive makes the information credible and who knows that others received it.
messages_and_shared_awareness.recognition_pattern: This subtheme appears when information travels through speech, labels, education, certification, disclosure, public announcements, advice, or observed costly actions. The key sign is that the model asks not just what was said, but why the receiver should believe it and whether everyone knows that others heard it too.
messages_and_shared_awareness.paper_reading_move: Classify the communication channel. Is the message cheap, costly, verifiable, public, private, or tied to the sender's type? Then compare sender incentives across types: would a low type want to imitate a high type, and would the high type pay a cost the low type would avoid? For common-knowledge claims, ask one more level: does each player know that the others know the same fact?
messages_and_shared_awareness.boundary_test: The transfer fails when all messages are treated alike. Cheap talk needs aligned interests or strategic discipline. Costly signaling needs a cost difference across types. Public information needs more than one person noticing it; coordination may require higher-order awareness. Without those distinctions, communication becomes decoration rather than evidence. The hardest cases are messages that are public but not credible, or credible to one receiver but not enough to coordinate a group. The question is always what belief actually moves.
